INTEREST OF AMICI CURIAE
Amici Curiae States of Arizona, Connecticut,
Delaware, Louisiana, Michigan, Minnesota,
Mississippi, New Mexico, Ohio, Oklahoma, Utah,
Washington, and West Virginia (“Amici States”)
submit this brief in support of Respondent State of
Florida and urge this Court to reaffirm its holding in
Williams v. Florida , 399 U.S. 78 (1970) . The Sixth
Amendment does not require a jury of exactly 12
people for serious offenses —i.e., any offense “where
imprisonment for more than six months is
authorized.” Baldwin v. New York , 399 U.S. 66, 69
(1970).
Most states  have criminal  justice systems that
permit juries of fewer  than 12 for some serious
offenses. Indeed, several of the Amici States changed
their laws to allow for juries of fewer than 12 in
reliance on Williams.
Overturning Williams would significantly disrupt
the crimi nal justice systems and pending criminal
trials and appeals in at least the seven states —
Arizona, Connecticut, Florida, Indiana, Louisiana,
Massachusetts, and Utah—that permit fewer than 12
person juries for felony offenses.1

1 See Ariz. Const. art. II, § 23 & Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 21 -102(A)–
(B) (requiring 12-person juries for criminal cases involving death
penalty or imprisonment for thirty years or more, and  providing
for eight -person juries for criminal cases in courts of record) ;
Conn. Const. art. I, § 19 & Conn. Gen. Stat. § 54-82(c) (requiring
12-person jury for capital cases, and providing for six-person jury
in all criminal cases not punished by death or life imprisonment);
Fla. Stat. § 913.10 (providing for six -person juries in all noncapital criminal cases); Ind. Code 35- 37-1-1(b) & 35 -50-2-1

2
In total, these seven states have hundreds of felony
convictions on direct review that may require a retrial
if Williams is overruled. These cases involve serious
felonies, including homicides, sexual offenses, and
violent crimes. Further, if Williams  is not upheld,
these states expec t substantial post -conviction
litigation, as well as significant additional
expenditures such as rebuilding courtrooms to
accommodate juries of 12 in jurisdictions that have
traditionally used panels of six or eight. It will also
pose greater challenges for rural communities that
already face difficulties in seating sufficient jurors.
But Petitioner Kian has not limited his briefing to
only “felony” offenses as he first presented in his
petition for writ of certiorari. Pet. at ii. Instead, his
merits brief seeks to expand the issue to all “serious
crime[s],” Pet. Br. at 1, 16 –24, which includes, at a
minimum, all crimes that carry a maximum sentence
of more than six months’ incarceration, see, e.g., Lewis
v. United States, 518 U.S. 322, 326 (1996) (holding an
offense is presumptively “petty” if it carries a
“maximum prison term of six months or less”); Pet. Br.
at 17 n.5 (appearing to agree that the term “serious

(mandating a 12-person jury for murder and Level 1 –5 felonies,
and six-person juries for any remaining crimes, including Level 6
felonies); La. Const. art. I, §  17(A) (stating six -person juries
required for cases “in which the punishment may be confinement
at hard labor o r confinement without hard labor for more than
six months”); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 218 §§ 26, 26A (providing for
six-person jury trials in district courts and Boston municipal
court department, which have jurisdiction over some felonies);
Utah Const. art. I,  § 10 & Utah Code Ann. § 78B -1-104(1)
(providing for juries of fewer than 12 in any non-capital criminal
case).

3
crime” is used to distinguish “petty offenses,” for
which there is no right to a jury trial and which applies
“where no more than six months imprisonment is
authorized” (citation and internal quotation marks
omitted)).
Thus, overturning Williams could affect another 21
states, all of which permit smaller juries for
misdemeanor offenses that carry maximum sentences
of more than six months’ incarceration. 2 The impact
might be even greater than that, because the six -
month line between petty and serious offenses, while
presumptive, is not dispositive. This Court has
acknowledged that even offenses with a  maximum
statutory penalty of fewer than six months may
require jury trials if the defendant demonstrates “that
any additional statutory penalties, viewed in
conjunction with the maximum authorized period of

Colo. Rev. Stat. §§ 18-1-406(a) & 18-1.3-501(a.5); Ga. Code Ann.
§§ 15-12-125 & 17-10-3(a); Idaho Code §§ 19-1902 & 18-2408(3);
Kan. Stat. Ann. §§ 21-6602(a) & 22-3404(1)–(2); Ky. Rev. Stat.
Ann. §§ 24A.110(2), 29A.280(1) & 532.090; Mich. Const. art. I,
§ 20; Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.8311 (a); Mich. Ct. R.  6.620(A);
Minn. Const. art. I, § 6; Minn. Stat. § 609.02(2)–(4); Minn. Gen.

§§ 10.30(1)(b) & 360.10(1); N.Y. Penal Law § 70.15(1); Ohio Crim.
R. 2(C), 23(B); Ohio Rev. Code §§ 2901.02(F), 3905.33, 3905.99(B)
& 6111.99; Okla. Stat. tit. 21, § 10 & tit. 22, § 601; Or. Rev. Stat.
§§ 136.210(2) & 161.615; Tex. Code Crim. Proc. Ann. art. 33.01;
Tex. Penal Code § 12.21; Va. Code Ann. §§ 18.2-11 & 19.2-262(B);
Wash. Const. art. I, § 21; Wash. Rev. Code 3.66.060; W. Va. Code
§§ 50-5-8(b), (d) & 61-3-13(b); Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 1 -11-119, 5-9-
129, 6-2-507(b) & 7-11-101.

4
incarceration, are so severe that they clearly reflect a
legislative determination that the offense in question
is a ‘serious’ one.” Blanton v. City of N. Las Vegas,
Nev., 489 U.S. 538, 543 (1989).
In short, under Kian’s expanded framing, this case
could affect more than half the states. Amici States
respectfully request that the Court give that impact
due weight in its stare decisis analysis.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
For all but two years of this nation’s history, this
Court’s precedents have clearly permitted states to
use juries of fewer than 12 persons in  criminal trials.
Several of  Amici States’ individual histories reflect
this tradition and exercise of self-determination. Until
1968, the Sixth Amendment’s jury trial right did not
apply to the states. See Duncan v. Louisiana, 391 U.S.
145, 149 (1968). Be fore Duncan, at least three states
experimented with smaller jury sizes in criminal trials
involving serious offenses. Florida, Louisiana, and
Utah enshrined smaller juries in their constitutions in
1875, 1879, and 1895, respectively. Then, just two
years after Duncan, this Court held that the Sixth
Amendment does not require 12 jurors in a criminal
case. See Williams, 399 U.S. at 102– 03. Instead,
Congress and the s tates had discretion to determine
the size of their juries. Id. at 103. In the years
immediately following Williams, several more states,
including Arizona, Indiana, Massachusetts, and
Connecticut, amended their constitutions or statutes
to reduce the size of juries in criminal trials.
Because states have historically utilized smaller
juries for at least some criminal offenses, whether the
Sixth Amendment requires a specific number of jurors

5
is a wholly different question than the unanimity
question this Court faced in Ramos v. Louisiana , 590
U.S. 83 (2020). In Ramos, this Court described the
unanimity requirement as an “ancient guarantee”
rooted in “400 years of English and American cases
requiring unanimity.” Id.  at 97, 100. No similar
ancient guarantee existed for the size of juries.
Williams correctly determined the Sixth
Amendment did not inc orporate every feature of the
common-law right to a jury trial, including the exact
number of jurors required. Stare decisis supports
retaining Williams, which “engag[ed] in a detailed
discussion of the original meaning of the Sixth
Amendment jury-trial right.” Ramos, 590 U.S. at 152
(Alito, J., dissenting). States have enacted laws,
amended constitutions, constructed courthouses, and
tried thousands of cases with smaller juries in reliance
on Williams. Overturning Williams now after more
than a half centur y of reliance would require a
substantial legislative and financial response from a
majority of states to adjust not only their laws, but
their infrastructure, to support 12 -person juries for
serious offense prosecutions. Thus, the reliance
interests here are nothing like the two- state outlier
situation in Ramos.
Upholding Williams reaffirms the principle that
the Sixth Amendment preserves the core right to a
jury trial without constitutionalizing every procedural
feature that existed at common law. Requir ing states
to adopt common law jury practices would improperly
constrain their sovereign authority to structure their
criminal justice systems.

6
ARGUMENT
I. Historical Development for Juries of Fewer
Than Twelve in Each State.
Seven states permit juries of few er than 12 for
offenses where a defendant faces more than a year of
incarceration. And 21 more states permit small juries
for misdemeanor offenses where a defendant faces up
to a year of incarceration. See supra note 2. The
histories of these laws reflect the unique approaches
states took when drafting their constitutions,
establishing their court systems, and defining their
criminal offenses.
A. Early Experimentation with Smaller
Juries.
In what would later become part of the modern
State of Connecticut, the New Haven colony, founded
in 1638, had no jury system at all. The Judicial and
Civil History of Connecticut  28, 68 (Hon. Dwight
Loomis & J. Gilbert Calhoun, eds., 1895). At the same
time, the Connecticut colony, which also later became
part of the modern State of Connecticut , permitted
magistrates to determine whether cases would require
6 or 12 jurors. Id.  at 127; The Code of 1650, Being a
Compilation of the Earliest Laws and Orders of the
General Court of Connecticut  60–62 (Silas Andrus,
1822). It was no t until after the two colonies merged
that 12-person juries were required. See  The Laws of
Connecticut: An Exact Reprint of the Original Edition
of 1673 37 (1865). The 12- person jury was statutorily
guaranteed only after statehood, though certain city
courts were permitted juries of six. See Acts and Laws
of the State of Connecticut, in America 5 (Timothy
Green, 1784); see also Acts and Laws of the State of

7
Connecticut, in America 71 (Hudson & Goodwin, 1796)
(Hartford City Court); id.  at 83 (Middletown City
Court); id. at 105 (New London City Court); id. at 114
(Norwich City Court). In 1818, Connecticut’s first
written constitution stated, “The right of trial by jury
shall remain inviolate.” See  Wesley W. Horton,
Annotated Debates of the 1818 Constitutional
Convention, 65 Conn. B.J. SI-1, SI-87, SI-103 (1991);
Conn. Const. of 1818 art. I, § 21.
Louisiana, established as a French territory in
1682, had a long tradition of trial without a jury.
See Warren Perrin, Revisiting the Genesis of French
Louisiana: It’ s No Coincidence the Civil Code Was
Adopted—We Ain’t Anglos! , 18 J. Civ. L. Stud.  5, 6
(2026); Judith M. Arnette, Jury Trial in Louisiana –
Implications of Duncan , 29 La. L. Rev.  118, 119–20
(1968). Under French rule, the Superior Council and
local inferior courts had jurisdiction over criminal
cases; under later Spanish rule, two alcaldes (a justice
of the peace ) sat as judges. H. Ward Fontenot, The
Louisiana Judicial System and the Fusion of Cultures,
63 La. L. Rev.  1149, 1150–53 (2003); Hays v. United
States, 175 U.S. 248, 258 (1899) . Even after the
Louisiana Purchase, the act of Congress establishing
the Territory of Orleans required jury trials only for
capital offenses. Act of March 26, 1804,  ch. 38, § 5, 2
Stat. 283, 284. As Louisiana approached state hood in
1811, Congress included the jury -trial right in the
enabling act. Louisiana Enabling Act, ch. 21, §  3, 2
Stat. 641, 642 (1811).
Louisiana’s 1868 Reconstruction constitution
provided for no jury trial in cases where the
punishment was “not necessarily hard labor or death”

8
and where the accused waived a jury trial and
proceeded to trial in a parish court.3 La. Const. of 1868
tit. IV, art. 87.4 Waiving a jury trial was significantly
speedier; parish courts met regularly, while the
district courts requi red for jury trials only met twice
per year. See State v. Lartigue , 29 La. Ann. 642, 645
(La. 1877).  Louisiana’s post-Reconstruction 1879
constitution later required  juries for criminal  cases
where the punishment was “not necessarily
imprisonment at hard l abor or death, ” but permitted
the General Assembly to set the jury size at fewer than
12. La. Const. of 1879 art. 7. The current constitution
provides for a jury of six when the punishment “may
be confinement at hard labor or confinement without
hard labor for more than six months.” La. Const. art.
I, § 17(A); State v. Breaux , 408 So. 3d 899, 904 (La.
2025) (explaining Louisiana’s “relative felony”
classification). Thus, six -member juries in Louisiana
continue to adjudicate serious offenses . See, e.g., La.
Stat. Ann. § 14:89.1(C)(1) (aggravated crime against
nature punishable by imprisonment “with or without
hard labor, for a term not less than five years nor more
than twenty years, or both”); State v. Doyle, 388 So.3d

3 “Hard labor” in Louisiana means state prison rather than
parish jail. See State v. Hamilton , 54 So. 482, 482 (La. 1911)
(explaining that “hard labor” means “hard labor to be performed
in the State Penitentiary”); see, e.g., State v. Flunder, 517 So.2d
1057, 1059 (La. Ct. App. 1987) (noting that hard labor is spent in
the state Department of Corrections in contrast with time spent
in parish jail).
4 This constitution was approved by Congress before
readmission to the United States. Act of June 25, 18 68, ch. 70,
§ 1, 15 Stat. 73, 73.

9
1226, 1228, 1246 (La. Ct. App. 2024) (12-year sentence
and 60-year exposure with six-person jury).
Florida’s smaller jury trials were first permitted
by an 1875 amendment to its constitution (which
permitted the number of jurors to be “fixed by law”),
and later by statute in 1877. See Gibson v.  State, 16
Fla. 291 (1877); Fla. Const.  of 1875 art. VI, § 12; Fla.
Laws 1877, ch. 3010, § 6.
In the mid -1800s, more adjustments began to
appear in state constitutions outside the context of
felonies or serious misdemeanors. When Iowa became
a state in 1846, its constitution permitted smaller
juries in “inferior courts,” and when Michigan adopted
its new constitution in 1850, it specifically permitted
smaller juries in criminal cases in courts “not of
record.” Iowa Const. of 1846 art. 1, § 9; Mich. Const. of
1850 art. VI, § 28. Similar exceptions appeared in
additional state constitutions in the mid to late 19th
century. See Colo. Const. art. I, § 23 (1876); Ga. Const.
of 1865 art. 5, § IV; Ky. Const. § 248 (1891); Mo. Const.
of 1875 art. II, §  28; Neb. Con st. of 1866 art. I, §  5
(1866); S.C. Const. art. IX, § 7 (1865); Tex. Const. art.
V, § 17 (1876); Wash. Const.  art. I, §  21 (1889); Wyo .
Const. art. I, § 9 (1889).
Utah enshrined smaller juries in its constitution
just before statehood. The issue, in both  the civil and
criminal context, was discussed several times during
the constitutional convention of 1895. The first
proposed language provided for 12 jurors for felony
cases and fewer for civil cases and non-felony offenses.
Official Report of the Proceed ings and Debates of the
Convention Assembled to Adopt a Constitution for the
State of Utah 274 (1895). One delegate who supported

10
a reduction argued there was no empirical basis to
conclude that 12 jury members were superior to nine,
and that nine jurors “ will prove just as effectual.” Id.
at 276. He also noted that, if Utah were admitted to
the United States , the additional taxation imposed
would “bear heavily upon the people of the Territory
of Utah,” and a jury of nine would result in “three less
men for which the State of Utah will have to pay.” Id.
One delegate also noted the practical burdens created
by maintaining a 12- person jury in a large, sparsely
populated territory. He explained that witnesses and
jurors in Utah’s four judicial districts often travelled
long distances to attend court and waited “five or six
days” while daily per-diem expenses accumulated. Id.
at 278–79. He argued “the expense of the jury system
is something enormous” and supported identifying
“ways to economize,” including the adoption of smaller
jury sizes. Id.
Due in part to its unique history as “the only state
in the Union which is known primarily because of the
religion of its leading denomination,” the Utah
territory unsuccessfully sought statehood in 1849,
1856, 1862, 1867, 1872, 1882, and 1887 before it was
finally admitted to the Union in 1895. Soc’y of
Separationists, Inc. v. Whitehead , 870 P.2d 916, 921 –
29 (Utah 1993) (internal quotation marks omitted).
Utah’s resulting first constitution was therefore
arguably one of t he most scrutinized constitutions in
all American history.
Yet despite this close scrutiny, President Grover
Cleveland proclaimed that Utah’s constitutional
draft—which included an eight -person-jury
provision—was “not repugnant to the Constitution of

11
the United States[,]” and Utah duly gained admission
to the Union and the authority to define its own jury -
trial structure. Proclamation 382, 29 Stat. 876, 876 –77
(1896). Utah law now provides for 12 jurors in capital
cases, eight jurors in noncapital cases with exposure
to 1 year of incarceration or more, and six jurors in
cases where the potential term of incarceration is
between 6 months and 1 year. See  Utah Code Ann.
§ 78B-1-104.
B. States Changing Jury Size After
Williams.
The remaining states that permit fel ony trials
with sub- 12-member juries made the change after
Williams. Connecticut was first. In 1971, the
Connecticut legislature discussed amending the
constitution to reduce the size of juries to six in civil
cases. This was to “make the jury system more
effective and more efficient.” 14 H.R. Proc., pt. 3, 1971
Sess., at 1036 (Conn.) (remarks of Rep. Carrozzella).
https://collections.ctdigitalarchive.org/node/1603380 .
Smaller juries meant not only less time selecting a
jury but also ensured that jurors wer e comfortable in
the courthouses, which were not equipped to
accommodate large panels. Id.  at 1035– 36.
Ultimately, in 1972, the voters of Connecticut
approved a constitutional amendment permitting the
legislature to establish the size of juries in both civ il
and criminal cases, and set the minimum number of
jurors at six in all but capital cases, which still
required 12. Conn. Const. art. I, § 19. The statutes
followed the next year. Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 54-82(c),
54-82b(c) (1973).

12
Massachusetts also considered a statutory change
to permit trials by juries of six beginning in 1971.
Opinion of the Justices , 271 N.E.2d 335, 336 (Mass.
1971). The state established six-person juries in some
district courts in 1972, then expanded that to all
divisions of the distr ict court in 1978. See
Commonwealth v. Nicoll , 897 N.E.2d 1226, 1231
(Mass. 2008). Current state laws provide for six -
member juries in certain felony cases tried in district
court, and the sentencing exposure is no more than 2.5
years. Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 218, §§ 26, 26A, 27; Mass.
Gen. Laws ch. 279, §§  19, 23; Commonwealth v.
Zawatsky, 670 N.E.2d 969, 972– 73 (Mass. App. Ct.
1996).
In 1972, then- Arizona State Senator Sandra
Day O’Connor introduced S.B. 1131. See  S.B.
1131, 30th Leg., 2nd Reg. Sess. (Ariz. 1972). The
bill provided for a 12 -member jury in cases
punishable by death and six -member juries in
other criminal cases. Introduced Version, S.B. 1131,
30th Leg., 2d Reg. Sess. (Jan. 20, 1972) ,
https://azmemory.azlibrary.gov/nodes/view/304245?sho
wbacklinknav=303128. It conditioned the enactment
on a constitutional amendment being passed by
popular vote. Id. State senators amended it to expand
12-person juries to cases where potential punishment
was death or 30 years or more of imprisonment, and
changed al l other criminal trials to eight -person
juries. Senate Engrossed Version, S.B. 1131, 30th
Leg., 2d Reg. Sess. (March 24, 1972). Ultimately,
voters approved a constitutional amendment
providing a floor of six jurors for cases where sentence
exposure was les s than 30 years. 1972 Arizona
Referendum and Initiative Publicity Pamphlet, at 11–

13
12. And the eight-person jury statute became law. See
1972 Ariz. Sess. Laws, ch. 94, §  2 (eff. Nov. 7, 1972);
Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 21–102(A), (B).
In 1973, a task force formed by the Department of
Justice recommended juries of fewer than 12. Nat ’l
Advisory Comm ’n on Crim . Just. Standards and
Goals, Report on Courts, Standard 4.14, Jury Size and
Composition, at 101 (1973). The task force concluded
that smaller juries could “provi de group deliberation
on the issue of guilt, resist outside influences, and
provide a fair possibility for obtaining a representative
cross section of the community,” and recommended
reductions to save time and money.  Id. Although the
federal courts still generally require 12-member juries
in criminal cases, in 1983, this Court amended Federal
Rule of Criminal Procedure 23 to permit a verdict from
11 jurors if the 12th is excused for good cause after
retiring to deliberate. Fed. R. Crim. P. 23(b)(3); see
also Fed. R. Crim. P. 23 advisory committee’s note to
1983 amendment (relying on Williams).
Indiana adopted smaller juries in 1975. The state
created a county court system that mandated six -
member juries in civil and misdemeanor criminal
cases; the state supreme court found it constitutional,
citing Williams. See In re Public Law No. 205 & Public
Law No. 309, 334 N.E.2d 659, 662– 63 (Ind . 1975);
O’Brien v. State, 422 N.E.2d 1266, 1268– 69 (Ind. Ct.
App. 1981). In 1979, the jurisdiction of county courts
was extended to include class D felonies. O’Brien, 422
N.E.2d at 1268. Now known as a “Level 6” felony,
these offenses can result in a prison term of 2.5 years.
See Ind. Code 35-50-2-7(b). A six -person jury is
mandated. Ind. Code 35-37-1-1.

14
Additionally, outside t he felony context, several
states with smaller jury trials for misdemeanors
expressly adopted changes relying on Williams . By
way of example, New York’s Court of Appeals altered
court procedure in 1970 in response to Duncan and
Williams, and the applicable statute was changed the
next year. See People v. Dargan , 261 N.E.2d 633, 714
(N.Y. 1970); see also N.Y. Laws 1971, ch. 815, §  4.
Minnesota altered its applicable statute in 1971.
See Baker v. State, 590 N.W.2d 636, 638 (Minn. 1999).
And Oregon voters altered their constitution in 1972.
See State v. Sagdal, 343 P.3d 226, 232 (Or. 2015).
In sum, there is no singular path states took to
seating smaller juries for felonies and other serious
offenses—Louisiana first joined the union with limited
jury trials du e to its past as a continental European
territory, while Utah joined the union with smaller
juries reflecting the cost concerns of a rural state in
the midst of the 1890s recession. Other states
experimented with smaller juries in inferior courts as
they organized, or re -organized, their court systems.
As Connecticut’s history demonstrates, the tradition
of experimentation goes back hundreds of years. This
Court’s decision in Williams then triggered additional
changes, resulting in what is now seven states with
sub-12-member juries in felony trials, and 21 more
states with smaller juries where the defendant faces
more than six months’ incarceration.
II. Williams Correctly Held the Sixth
Amendment Does Not Require 12- Member
Juries in the States.
“In the view of the Court that is considering
whether to overrule, the precedent must be

15
egregiously wrong as a matter of law in order for the
Court to overrule it.” Ramos , 590 U.S. at 122
(Kavanaugh, J., concurring in part). Williams ’s
reasoning is sound and it is not egregiously wrong.
The Sixth Amendment’s text does not contain a 12-
member jury requirement. U.S. Const. amend. VI.
Williams thoroughly examined the history of the Sixth
Amendment, as  incorporated by the Fourteenth
Amendment, and correctly concluded that history does
not require state criminal juries to be composed of 12
members. See Williams , 399 U.S. at 92– 100;
see also Ramos, 590 U.S. at 152 (Alito, J., dissenting)
(stating Williams engaged in a “detailed discussion of
the original meaning of the Sixth Amendment jury -
trial right”). As Williams noted, the “relevant
constitutional history casts considerable doubt on the
easy assumption in our past decisions that  if a given
feature existed in a jury at common law in 1789, then
it was necessarily preserved in t he Constitution.” Id.
at 92.
Williams rightly decided that— in the face of an
ambiguous historical record —it could not conclude
that the 12- person jury was a constitutional
requirement. 399 U.S. at 102– 03. That holding left
considerations about the proper number of jurors “to
Congress and the s tates, unrestrained by an
interpretation of the Sixth Amendment that would
forever dictate the precise number that can constitute
a jury.” Id.  at 103. Indeed, “something more than
ambiguous historical evidence is required” before this
Court will overturn precedent. See Gamble v. United
States, 587 U.S. 678, 691 (2019) (internal quotation
marks omitted). Williams  reasonably interpreted the

16
Sixth Amendment. Amy C. Barrett, Stare Decisis and
Due Process, 74 U. Colo. L. Rev. 1011, 1058 (2003) (“If
a precedent reasonably interprets a constitutional or
statutory provision, a successor court should not
substitute its judgment for that of the predecessor
court.”).
Kian asks the Court to adopt language from
Thompson v. Utah, 170 U.S. 343 (1898), Pet. Br. at 2,
6, 10, 22, but that is asking too much. In Thompson ,
the Court failed to consider whether the Framers
intended “every feature of the jury as it existed at
common law—whether incidental or essential to that
institution—[to be] necessarily  included in the
Constitution wherever that document referred to a
‘jury.’” Williams, 399 U.S. at 91.  Thompson did not
engage in any originalist analysis at all. Rather, it
simply assumed, without citation to authority, that
the Framers “were of opinion that life and liberty,
when involved in criminal prosecutions, would not be
adequately secured except through the unanimous
verdict of twelve jurors.” 170 U.S. at 353.
Williams found Thompson’s reasoning to be
inconsistent with the Constitution’s original meaning.
399 U.S. at 90– 92; see also id. at 107 (Black, J.,
concurring in part) (“The broad implications in early
cases indicating that only a body of 12 members could
satisfy the Sixth Amendment requirement arose in
situations where the issue was not squarely presented
and were based, in my opinion, on an improper
interpretation of that amendment.”). And later cases
repeating Thompson’s language , “often in dictum,”
failed to engage in any meaningful analysis to discern
whether the number of jurors was, in fact, an

17
“essential element” of the jury-trial right. Id. at 91–92
(citing Patton v. United States , 281 U.S. 276, 288
(1930), Rassmussen v. United States, 197 U.S. 516, 519
(1905), and Maxwell v. Dow, 176 U.S. 581, 586 (1900)).
Thompson’s Sixt h Amendment analysis was not
the only way in which that case drifted from the
Constitution’s original meaning.  Significantly—20
years after Williams —the Court expressly overruled
Thompson’s Ex Post Facto Clause analysis because it
was inconsistent “with the understanding of the term
‘ex post facto law’ at the time the Constitution was
adopted.” Collins v. Youngblood , 497 U.S. 37, 47
(1990). While overruling  Thompson, the Court
reaffirmed Williams. Collins, 497 U.S . at 52 n.4
(noting that Thompson ’s holding “that the Sixth
Amendment requires a jury panel of 12 persons” was
rendered “obsolete” by Williams).
III. The Stare Decisis  Doctrine Compels
Adherence to Williams.
“Stare decisis promotes the evenhanded,
predictable, and consistent development of legal
principles, fosters reliance on judicial decisions, and
contributes to the actual and perceived integrity of the
judicial process. ” Gamble, 587 U.S. at 691 (internal
quotation marks omitted) ; see also Kimble v. Marvel
Entertainment, LLC, 576 U.S. 446, 455 (2015) (“ Stare
decisis—in English, the idea that today’s Court should
stand by yesterday’s decisions —is a foundation stone
of the rule of law.”) (internal quotation omitted) . “[A]
departure from precedent demands special
justification.” Gamble, 587 U.S. at 691 (i nternal
quotation marks omitted).

18
Generally, when considering whether to apply
stare decisis, this Court considers “the quality of [the
past decision’s] reasoning, the workability of the rule
it established, its consistency with other related
decisions, a nd … reliance on the decision.” Knick v.
Township of Scott, 588 U.S. 180, 203 (2019) (internal
quotation omitted). In addition to Williams being
correctly decided, the other factors weigh strongly in
favor of upholding Williams.
A. This Court Has Repeatedly Affirmed
Williams Throughout the Past Half -
Century.
Kian contends that Williams is an outlier, Pet. Br.
at 29, but this Court’s precedent shows the opposite.
Unlike the plurality opinion in Apodaca v. Oregon, 406
U.S. 404 (1972) , this Court has not been “s tudiously
ambiguous” or “inconsistent” about what Williams
held. Ramos, 590 U.S. at 95–96.
In the 56  years since Williams was decided, this
Court has reaffirmed and extended its holding on
several occasions. See United States v. Gaudin , 515
U.S. 506, 510 n.2 (1995) (endorsing Williams’s
analysis while holding that the jury’s role in
determining guilt, not the number of jurors, is
indispensable to the right to trial by jury); Burch v.
Louisiana, 441 U.S. 130, 134 –37 (1979) (detailing
development of Williams and related cases); Ballew v.
Georgia, 435 U.S. 223 (1978) (expressly reaffirming
Williams while holding constitutional minimum jury
size is six); Ludwig v. Massachusetts, 427 U.S. 618,
625–26 (1976) (discussing Williams and upholding
constitutionality of Massachusetts’s two-tiered jury
system).

19
Civil jury trials in the federal courts rest on a
foundation built by Williams. In the wake of Williams,
more than 50 federal district courts adopted local rules
providing for six -person civil juries.  See Colgrove v .
Battin, 413 U.S. 149, 150 n.1 (1973); H. Richmond
Fisher, The Seventh Amendment and the Common
Law: No Magic in Numbers, 56 F.R.D. 507, 535– 42
(1973) (cited in footnote 1 of Colgrove).
Colgrove considered a challenge to the District of
Montana’s six-person civil jury rule. 413 U.S. at 149–
50. Relying heavily on  Williams, the Court held that
just as the Sixth Amendment does not
constitutionalize a right to a 12- person jury in
criminal cases, neither does the Seventh Amendment
in civil cases. Id. at 156–58.
In 1991, this Court amended Federal Rule of Civil
Procedure 48 to allow six -person juries nationwide.
See Fed. R. Civ. P. 48(a). Given Colgrove’s heavy
reliance on Williams , overruling Williams could call
into doubt a great number of federal civil jury
verdicts—and current widespread practice —
nationwide.
This Court has also relied on Williams to require
a minimum of six people on a criminal jury. In Ballew
(five years after Colgrove), the Court restated
Williams’s holding and endorsed it again: “Rather
than requiring 12 members, [] the Sixth Amendment
mandate[s] a jury only of sufficient size to promote
group deliberation, to insulate members from outside
intimidation, and to provide a representative cross -
section of the community.” Ballew , 435 U.S. at 23 0
(citing Williams, 399 U.S. at 100). The Court then
noted that Williams and Colgrove “generated a

20
quantity of scholarly work on jury size.” Id. at 231. But
those writings did not “draw or identify a bright line
below which the number of jurors would not be able to
function as required by the standards enunciated  in
Williams.” Id. at 231– 32. However, “they raise[d]
significant questions about the wisdom and
constitutionality of a reduction below six.” Id . at 232.
The Court thoroughly examined those concerns ,
“reaffirm[ed] [its] holding in Williams ,” and decided
the post-Williams studies compelled a conclusion that
“the purpose and functioning of the jury in a criminal
trial is seriously impaired, and to a constitutional
degree, by a reduction in size to below six members.”
Id. at 232–39.
Because this Court has not only reaffirmed but
extended Williams, stare decisis provides powerful
support for maintaining Williams  intact. See
Michigan v. Bay Mills Indian Cmty. , 572 U.S. 782,
798–99 (2014) (affirming precede nt when it “was no
one-off” and it had been subsequently relied on);  see
also Barrett, 74 U. Colo. L. Rev. at 1069 (“The fact that
a long line of predecessor courts has affirmed and
reaffirmed a proposition is a valid indication that the
proposition is sound.”).
B. Williams Has Not Caused Significant
Negative Jurisprudential or Real -World
Consequences.
Kian contends Williams has caused
jurisprudential difficulties and negative real- world
consequences. Pet. Br. at 34–37. Not so. In conducting
this inquiry, cour ts “may consider jurisprudential
consequences,” such as “workability,” “consistency and
coherence with other decisions,” and “the precedent’s

21
real-world effects on the citizenry, not just its effects
on the law and the legal system.” Ram os, 590 U.S. at
122 (Kavanaugh, J., concurring in part).
As an initial matter, Williams’s holding that 12-
member juries are not mandated by the Sixth
Amendment is workable, which Kian does not dispute.
Williams and its progeny allow states flexibility in
trying criminal jury trials by deciding whether to
empanel 6, 8, 12, or some other number of jurors.
Williams’s rule is clear and “can be understood and
applied in a consistent and predictable manner.”
Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization , 597
U.S. 215, 280– 81 (2022). Indeed, both the state s and
federal courts have readily adapted to Williams in a
manner that leads to predictable jury sizes.
Similarly, in 1983, this Court —relying on
Williams—approved Federal Rule of Criminal
Procedure 23(b)(3), which allows a jury of 11 to return
a verdict if there is good cause to excuse a juror during
deliberation. See Fed. R. Crim. P. 23(b), Advisory
Comm. Note to 1983 Amendments. The Advisory
Committee specifically stated that “the alignment of
the Court and especially the separate opinion by
Justice Powell in [Apodaca] makes it at best uncertain
whether less -than-unanimous verdicts would be
constitutionally permissible in federal trials,” but “it
hardly follows that a requirement of unanimity of a
group slightly less than 12 is s imilarly suspect.” Id.
(internal citation omitted). Consistent with Rule
23(b)(3), federal courts have routinely upheld 11 -
person verdicts. See United States v. Golobic, 170
F.4th 515, 518– 19 (6th Cir. 2026) ( upholding 11-
person verdict under Rule 23(b)(3 )); United States v.

22
Paulino, 445 F.3d 211, 225– 26 (2d Cir. 2006) ( same);
United States v. Hively, 437 F.3d 752, 766–67 (8th Cir.
2006) (same); United States v. Geffrard , 87 F.3d 448,
450–52 (11th Cir. 1996) (same); United States v. Acker,
52 F.3d 509, 515– 16 ( 4th Cir. 1995) (same); United
States v. Egbuniwe , 969 F.2d 757, 760– 63 (9th Cir.
1992) (same); United States v. O’Brien , 898 F.2d 983,
986 (5th Cir. 1990) (same) ; see also United States v.
Johnson, 117 F.4th 28, 40– 43 (2d Cir. 2024) (holding
that Rule 23(b)(3) error does not affect a constitutional
or substantial right).
Williams also did not create other jurisprudential
difficulties. Kian points to Balle w, but acknowledges
that “Ballew declined to overrule Williams ,” Pet. Br.
at 31– 32. The only concer n the concurring Justices
expressed with the majority’s approach was that the
validity and methodology of the statistical studies the
Court considered had not been subjected to the
adversarial process, and those Justices questioned the
wisdom of relying on them at all. Ballew, 435 U.S. at
245–46 (Powell, J., concurring). Notably, the same
Justices maintained the Sixth Amendment should not
have been fully incorporated in the first place. Id.
Further, Kian cannot show that Williams has
resulted in other nega tive real- world consequences.
See Ramos, 590 U.S.  at 122 (Kavanaugh, J.,
concurring in part ). The non -unanimous juries
permitted by Apodaca allowed for convictions where
unanimous juries would have hung or at least
deliberated more, essentially “sanction[ing] the
conviction at trial or by guilty plea of some defendants
who might not be convicted under the proper
constitutional rule.” Id.  at 126 (Kavanaugh, J.,

23
concurring in part). No study was necessary to
illustrate that real-world consequence.
Here, Kian and several amici  point to academic
studies, and to Ballew , but these  arguments are
speculative at best. Kian further alleges, without
evidence, that  Williams “does real harm to public
perception of the jury as a legitimate, representative
body,” Pet. Br. at 35. But in Connecticut and Arizona,
it was the voters who approved the reduction in jury
sizes in 1971 and 1972. And states like Utah and
Florida have continuously used sub- 12-person juries
since the late 19th century; no one alive in these states
today has ever known another system. If there truly
were widespread public concerns about sub-12-person
juries, as Kian suggests, then surely Kian would be
able to offer some evidence of the existence of that
public concern over the past century. He offers none.
C. The States’ Significant Reliance
Interests Support Adherence t o
Williams.
Finally, stare decisis counsels against overruling
Williams because doing so would upset significant
reliance interests of  not only Florida but at least six
other states, and many more if the Court were to adopt
Petitioner’s expanded framing of the question
presented to include jury trials for “serious crimes.”
Cf. Ramos, 590 U.S. at  108–09 (concluding reliance
interests were not as weighty when “only two States
are potentially affected by our judgment”).

24
1. Overturning Williams would
require an extensive legislative
response.
Stare decisis has added force when the legislature
has acted in reliance upon a previous decision because
overruling such a decision would require an extensive
legislative response . See Hilton v. S.C. Pub. Rys.
Comm’n, 502 U.S. 197, 202 (1991). As detailed above,
multiple state legislatures (and state electorates)
amended their statutes or constitutions in reliance on
Williams. Revisiting Williams and imposing a 12 -
member jury requirement would invalidate state
constitutional provisions  or statutes  in at least six
other states, and potentially up to 28  states. Such
sweeping invalidation of state laws would require a
substantial legislative overhaul for a majority of
jurisdictions.
Additionally, pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 2074,
Congress might need to approve an amendment to
Rule 23, Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure, which
permits the district court to accept a verdict from a
jury of 11, “even without a stipulation by the parties.”
At least two other jurisdictions with similar provisions
would also require amendments to those rules. See
D.C. Super. Ct. R. Crim. P. 23(b)(3); Mass. Gen. Laws
ch. 234A, § 68. Kian argues this Court need not resolve
the constitutionality of Rule 23 because it involves
procedures applicable to emergencies but provides no
authority to support that assertion. Pet. Br. at 13 n.4.
Nor does  he explain why a constitutional provision
would carry less force after the jury is sworn, but
before it returns its verdict, particularly when the rule

25
allows the trial court to order an 11 -person jury
without the consent (or waiver) of the defendant.
2. Overruling Williams would trigger
significant fiscal impacts.
Overruling Williams would also require an other
legislative response  from affected jurisdictions to
address the fiscal impacts of increasing jury sizes. At
least three fiscal impacts would result from
overturning Williams: (1) courthouses built for juries
of fewer than 12 would need to be reconstructed  to
accommodate larger juries, (2) juror compensation
funds would need additional appropriations, and
(3) affected jurisdictions would see an immediate
increase in retrials and post -conviction relief
litigation.
1. In affected jurisdictions, many state and
municipal courtrooms are simply not built to handle
12-person juries for every serious offense. Some amici
suggest otherwise, pointing to the states’ practice of
trying at least some cases by a jury of 12 or seating
alternate jurors. See, e.g. , Brief Amicus Curiae of the
Utah Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers in
Support of Petitioner, at 20 –21; Amicus Brief of the
Florida Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers and
the Florida Public Defender Association, Inc. in
Support of Petitioner, at 24–25. But the fact that each
state holds at least some 12 -person trials does not
mean that every courtroom is built for a jury of 12.
This is especially true for courthouses designated to
handle misdemeanor offenses, and for states like Utah
and Florida, which reserve 12-person juries only for a
handful of capital trials each year. See, e.g. , State of
Utah Judiciary, Utah Judicial Facility Design

26
Standards 100 (2021) , https://perma.cc/JDJ2-3BTA
(providing that the “standard jury box” in Utah
courthouses “should acco mmodate eight jurors” and
that “[o]nly one courtroom in each facility needs to
accommodate a 14 person jury box”).
Nor does the practice of seating alternate jurors
necessarily mean every courtroom is equipped to
handle 12-person juries. States are not sea ting up to
six alternate jurors for every trial. Rather, the
common practice is to seat one to two alternates. See
William R. Pabst, Jr., Statistical Studies of the Costs
of Six -Man Versus Twelve -Man Juries , 14 Wm. &
Mary L. Rev. 326, 328 (1972) (“In practice, the number
selected for the six-man jury was either seven or eight
(six, plus one or two alternates)[.]”).
In many states, at least some portion of the jury
boxes and deliberation rooms likely cannot
accommodate 12-person juries, plus alternates. Jury
assembly rooms built in anticipation of smaller pools
of prospective jurors may likewise struggle to
accommodate larger jury pools required for a 12 -
person jury. Even spectator seating may need to be
adjusted in some courtrooms to accommodate larger
groups of prospective jurors during jury selection.
See, e.g., Off. of the State Court Adm’r, 19th Judicial
District of Colorado Weld County Facility and Space
Needs Assessment with 20 -Year Projections, App.
Section C: Colo. Jud. Space Standards and Guidelines
at 104 (2026), https://perma.cc/5S7G-9MYW (“The size
of the spectator seating area is often determined by
the size of the jury panel that needs to be seated
during voir dire.”).

27
In this respect, the reliance factors at issue here
are far more substantial t han in Ramos. There, this
Court reasoned that Louisiana and Oregon had not
claimed “anything like the prospective economic,
regulatory, or social disruption litigants seeking to
preserve precedent usually invoke.” Ramos , 590 U.S.
at 84. And this Court note d that “[n]o one, it seems,
has signed a contract, entered a marriage , purchased
a home, or opened a business based on the expectation
that, should a crime occur, at least the accused may be
sent away by a 10-to-2 verdict.” Id.
Here, a decision contrary to Williams would likely
require extensive changes to many courthouses . A
courthouse is a generational investment, reflecting
the community’s commitment to the justice system
and its expectation that the courthouse will serve for
decades to come. Since Williams, federal, state,
county, and municipal courthouses across the country
have been built with at least some courtrooms
designed for juries of fewer than 12. See, e.g. , Admin.
Off. of the U.S. Courts, U.S. Courts Design Guide 132
1991), https://perma.cc/5 F6G-YR98 (recommending
that “[i]n the 6-member jury trial courtrooms, 8 juror
seats should be provided in the jury box”).
In fact, even state courthouses built before
Williams were not necessarily designed with the Sixth
Amendment right in mind because thi s Court did not
hold that the Sixth Amendment applied to the states
until Duncan in 1968. See, e.g., 14 H.R. Proc., pt. 3,
1971 Sess., at 1035– 37 (Conn.) (remarks by two
representatives in support of reducing juror size to
alleviate current problems with small rooms, with one
representative describing “[t]he conditions the jurors

28
are asked to serve under [as] almost …  criminal”). If
this Court  overrules Williams and holds that  all
serious offenses require 12 -person juries, the fiscal
impact of rebuilding  courthouses to accommodate
those larger juries will likely be substantial. This
fiscal impact stands in stark contrast to Ramos, where
overturning Apodaca had no effect on the
infrastructure of the affected states.
2. State legislatures will need to either
appropriate additional funds to cover the increased
costs to seat larger juries or impose higher court fees
to account for the additional costs in administering
jury trials.
Because of Connecticut’s unique jury selection
process, which was adopted after j ury sizes were
reduced from 12 to 6, the cost to Connecticut will be
significant. In Connecticut, there is a constitutional
and statutory guarantee to individually voir dire each
venireperson outside the presence of other
venirepersons. See Conn. Const. art I, § 19 (“The right
to question each juror individually by counsel shall be
inviolate”); Conn. Gen. Stat. §  54-82f. These rights
were first enshrined in Connecticut’s state
constitution following the 1972 constitutional
amendment reducing jury sizes to six persons. Wesley
W. Horton, The Connecticut State Constitution 91
(Oxford University Press , 2d ed. 2012) . Given this
required procedure and that the re is no fixed time
limit for voir dire, see State v. Roberson, 376 A.2d 1087,
1088 (Conn. 1977), jury sel ection can take parties
multiple days, even weeks, to select six -person juries,
and multiple weeks, if not months, to select twelve -
person juries, juries, see, e.g., State v. Komisarjevsky,

29
258 A.3d 1166, 1187 (Conn. 2021)  (noting that jury
selection “bega n on March 16, 2011, and ended on
June 14, 2011”).  Increasing the size of juries in
Connecticut will slow criminal proceedings, utilize
more judicial resources, and delay parties’ access to
justice.
Requiring 12- person juries will impose even
greater burdens on rural counties, many of which
already struggle to empanel juries in high -profile
cases. For example, in a sexual assault case in
Beaver County, Utah, which had a population of just
6,005, the Utah Court of Appeals ordered retrial in
a different venu e because “a few of the jurors knew
one another, several jurors knew either the
prosecutor or one of the State’s witnesses, and a
majority of the jurors knew [the victim’s] family.”
State v. Stubbs , 84 P.3d 837, 840 (Utah Ct. App.
2004), aff’d, 123 P.3d 40 7 (Utah 2005). And
Beaver County is not alone. According to recent
census data, many states have counties or parishes
with populations of less than 10,000, including:
Minnesota (21 counties), Oklahoma (20), Mississippi
(15), West Virginia (12), Utah (9), Louisiana (8),
Michigan (8), New Mexico (8), Washington (4),
and Arizona (1). See U.S. Census Bureau, County
Population Totals and Components of Change:
2020-2025 2025, https://www.census.gov/data/tables/timeseries/demo/popest/2020s-counties-total.html (providing
each state’s county populations). Kian insists that 12-
person juries are necessary to ensure that juries
“include a true cross -section of the community.” Pet .
Br. at 35. But ironically, his rule is likely to decrease
citizen representation by fo rcing more changes of

30
venue away from small, tight-knit communities where
assembling juries is already a significant challenge.
3. Overruling Williams would also initiate a wave
of litigation. At a minimum, all defendants convicted
of a serious offense by a jury of fewer than 12 whose
cases are still on direct appeal would be entitled to
press this claim. Utah currently has approximately
254 non-capital felony cases which were tried before
eight-person juries and are currently on direct
appeal, and which wo uld therefore be similarly
threatened by overruling Williams. Arizona estimates
approximately 180 cases currently on direct appeal
could be similarly affected (about 40% of the criminal
felony appeals). Connecticut estimates such a ruling
could affect approximately 70% of its felony cases. And
retrials could be required not only in states that have
felony convictions, but also the states that have fewer
than 12- person juries for misdemeanor offenses
carrying a sentence of more than six months’
imprisonment.
The Ramos majority dismissed warnings from the
dissent that overturning Apodaca would “provoke a
‘crushing’ ‘tsunami’ of follow -on litigation,” as an
“overstatement … intended for dramatic effect.”
Ramos, 590 U.S. at 108. It further dismissed warnings
that if its ruling were made retroactive, finalized
convictions could be overturned through collateral
review. Id. at 109. But the last six years have
confirmed Oregon’s prediction that hundreds of cases
could be reversed. Although this Court ruled that
Ramos was not retroactive under its own retroactivity
test, see Edwards v. Vannoy, 593 U.S. 255 (2021), the
Oregon Supreme Court found the holding was

31
retroactive, see Watkins v. Ackley , 523 P.3d 86, 103
(Or. 2022).
Recognizing Watkins would call into question
hundreds of convictions, the Oregon Legislature
appropriated about $4.1 million toward litigation
related to cases impacted by Watkins and Ramos
and directed the Oregon Public Defense Commission
to provide a report on caseloads and costs. See Or.
Leg. Fiscal Off., 2025 Joint Comm. on Ways and
Means, Analysis, Pub. Def. Comm., Nonunanimous
Jury Convictions , https://perma.cc/5C52-57BA. The
commission’s report identified “649 cases or petitions”
and calculated “$2,532,358 in costs related to the
[post-conviction relief] cases under Watkins or
Ramos.” Id. Notably, these estimates did not account
for prosecution or judicial expenditures, and did not
capture the expenditures for retrials, which the
defense commission treated as “newly filed cases.” Id.
The Ore gon Legislature also ordered a similar
report from the Oregon Department of Justice. See Or.
Leg. Fiscal Off., 2025 Joint Comm. on Ways and
Means, Analysis, Dep’t of Justice, Nonunanimous Jury
Conviction Caseloads, https://perma.cc/75RC-MH2T.
The departmen t reported that as of February 2025,
more than 700 direct appeals raised claims related to
Ramos, and almost 500 cases were reversed at least in
part. Id. at 3. Further, the issue was raised in
approximately 850 post-conviction petitions. Id.
Unlike Ramos, which involved convictions from
just two states, here the Court faces a far larger
number of convictions that could be unsettled if it
overturns Williams. Retrial may not be possible in
every case, especially if the holding is made

32
retroactive by either t his Court or a state supreme
court. Key witnesses may no longer be available,
evidence may not have been retained once a conviction
was deemed final, or a victim may refuse to testify to
avoid retraumatization. See Summerville v. Warden ,
641 A.2d 1356, 137 1 (Conn. 1994) (recognizing “the
fact that in many cases an order for a new trial may in
reality reward the accused with complete freedom
from prosecution because of the debilitating effect of
the passage of time on the state’s evidence”). These are
not trivial concerns. Cf. Ariz. Const. art. II, § 2.1
(providing that victims have a right to “prompt and
final conclusion of the case after the conviction and
sentence”); Conn. Const. art. I, § 8(b)(2) (providing
that victims have a “right to timely disposition  of the
case following arrest of the accused, provided no right
of the accused is abridged”); Utah Code Ann. § 77-37-
3(1)(h) (“Victims and witnesses, particularly children,
should have a speedy disposition of the entire criminal
justice process.”).
IV. States Should Determine Procedures for
Criminal Jury Trials, Including the Size of
Juries.
Williams’s holding also comports with the settled
proposition that s tates should be given flexibility to
administer their criminal justice systems. See Oregon
v. Ice, 555 U.S. 160, 170 (2009) (“Beyond question, the
authority of States over the administration of their
criminal justice systems lies at the core of their
sovereign status.”); Ludwig, 427 U.S.  at 630 (“The
modes of exercising federal constitutional rights have
traditionally been left, within limits, to state
specification.”).

33
The Sixth Amendment did not reduce the right to
a jury trial to an enumerated list of procedures to
follow. The states must, of course, adhere to the core
right of a jury trial, but states should not be bound by
procedures simply because they may have been
commonplace when the Sixth Amendment was
adopted. Williams, 399 U.S. at 100– 03 (“To read the
Sixth Amendment as forever codifying a feature so
incidental to the real purpose of the Amendment is to
ascribe a blind formalism to the Framers which would
require considerably more evidence than we have been
able to discover in the history and language of the
Constitution or in the reasoning of our past decisions.”).
If th is Court were to hold that  the Sixth
Amendment requires 12 -member juries then what
other common law procedures must states follow? See
Ramos, 590 U.S. at 153– 54 (Alito, J., dissenting)
(“Unless one is willing to freeze in place late 18th -
century practice, it is necessary to find a principle to
distinguish between the features that were
incorporated and those that were not.”). Surely states
are not required to mimic all procedures from a jury
trial at the founding.
For example, t he number of peremptory
challenges “was settled by the  common law at thirty -
five.” United States v. Wood, 299 U.S. 123, 145 (1936)
(internal quotation marks omitted) . But states have
developed different procedures and rules governing
peremptory challenges.  In fact, Arizona has become
the first state to abolis h peremptory challenges.
Ariz. Sup. Ct. Order R -21-0020 (Aug. 30, 2021) . This
Court has previously recognized “it is for the State to
determine the number of peremptory challenges

34
allowed and to define their purpose and the matter of
their exercise.” Ross v. Oklahoma, 487 U.S. 81, 89
(1988). If Williams is overturned, does this start to call
into question this other precedent?
And what about the common law practice of juries
de medietate linguae—meaning “in civil and criminal
trials involving minorities, of  juries consisting half of
natives and half of foreigners.” See Deborah A.
Ramirez, The Mixed Jury and the Ancient Custom of
Trial by Jury De Medietate Linguae: A History and a
Proposal for Change, 74 B.U. L. Rev. 777, 781– 82,
789–94 (Nov. 1994). This “anc ient rule” “no longer
obtains.” Wood, 299 U.S. at 145. But must it be revived
because it was a feature of a jury trial at common law?
At common law, parties were disqualified from
testifying in their own cases. See Joel N. Bodansky,
The Abolition of the Party -Witness Disqualification:
An Historical Survey, 70 Ky. L. J. 91, 91–93 (1981–82).
This rule was abolished between the late 1840s and
1890s, see Kenneth S. Abraham, The Common Law
Prohibition on Party Testimony and the Development
of Tort Liability , 95 Va. L. Rev.  489, 495–96 (2009);
was that unconstitutional?
Common law jury trials included denying jurors
“meat, drink, fire, [and] candle” until the jury
unanimously returned a verdict. 3 William Blackstone,
Commentaries *375. And trial judges summarized the
evidence and told “jurors which witnesses they found
most credible, and why.” David A . Sklansky,
Evidentiary Instructions and the Jury as Other , 65
Stan. L. Rev.  407, 413 (2013). Kian does not offer a
limiting principle for why the states must follow certain
features of common law jury trial but not others. See

35
Ramos, 590 U.S. at 153–54 & n.26 (Alito, J., dissenting)
(stating the Ramos  majority did not “identify any
principle” for determining which common law jury trial
features were incorporated by the Sixth Amendment).
Affirming Williams, thus, also reiterates that states
retain control over the procedures of their criminal trials.
As this Court has oft repeated, “the Constitution ‘has
never been thought [to] establish this Court as a rulemaking organ for the promulgation of state rules of
criminal procedure.’” Smith v. Robbins, 528 U.S. 259, 274
(2000) (quoting Spencer v. Texas, 385 U.S. 554, 564 (1967)).
CONCLUSION
This Court should affirm.
